prompt: Which three basic components do most lasers consist of?

choices.text: Gain medium, pump source, optical cavity
Gain medium, flash lamp, diffraction grating
choices.why: A flash lamp is only one kind of pump, and a grating appears only in tunable lasers. The three basic parts are a gain medium, a pump source and an optical cavity.

choices.text: Pump source, focusing lens, photodetector
choices.why: Lenses and detectors aren't among the basic parts. A laser needs a gain medium to emit, a pump to energize it, and an optical cavity to amplify the light.

choices.text: Gain medium, optical cavity, cooling jacket
choices.why: Cooling isn't one of the three basic components. The third is the pump source, which supplies energy to the gain medium.

explanation: Most lasers have a gain medium, from which light of a specific frequency is emitted; a pump source, which provides energy to the gain medium; and an optical cavity, in which the light is amplified by passing repeatedly through the gain medium.

prompt: What is the gain medium (active medium) of a laser?

choices.text: Atoms or molecules that undergo stimulated emission
The partly reflecting mirror that lets the beam escape
choices.why: That's the output coupler, part of the optical cavity. The gain medium is the collection of atoms or molecules that can undergo stimulated emission.

choices.text: The power supply that delivers the energy
choices.why: That's the pump source. The gain medium is the material whose atoms or molecules are excited and then emit by stimulated emission.

choices.text: A filter that removes unwanted wavelengths
choices.why: No filter is meant. The gain medium is the collection of atoms or molecules that can undergo stimulated emission and so emits the laser light.

explanation: The gain medium, or active medium, is a collection of atoms or molecules that can undergo stimulated emission. The laser light comes from a transition between two of its quantized states.

prompt: In which physical states can a laser's gain medium be?

choices.text: Gas, liquid or solid
Only solid crystals
choices.why: Ruby is a solid, but gases (such as Ar^+) and liquid dye solutions are used too. A gain medium can be a gas, a liquid or a solid.

choices.text: Only gases at low pressure
choices.why: Gas lasers are common, but ruby and Nd:YAG are solids and dye lasers use liquid solutions. All three states are possible.

choices.text: Only pure substances, never solutions
choices.why: Dye lasers use a dye dissolved in a solution. The gain medium can be a pure substance or a solution, in any of the three states.

explanation: The active medium can be in a gaseous, liquid or solid form, and it can be a pure substance or a solution. Examples are gas mixtures, dye solutions and ruby crystals.

prompt: Why is laser light always monochromatic?

choices.text: It comes from one transition between quantized states
A filter inside the cavity absorbs every other color
choices.why: No filter is involved. The light is created by a single transition between two quantized states of the gain medium, so it has one frequency.

choices.text: The pump source itself emits only a single wavelength
choices.why: The pump frequency differs from the laser frequency, so it doesn't set the color. One color comes from the single transition between two quantized states.

choices.text: Its light waves all stay exactly in phase with one another
choices.why: Being in phase is coherence, a different property. Laser light is monochromatic because it comes from a transition between two quantized states.

explanation: The emitted light of a laser is created by the transition between two quantized states of the gain medium, so it has a single frequency: laser light is always monochromatic.

prompt: Ruby is corundum, Al2O3, in which some of the Al^3+ ions are replaced. Which ion's electronic structure lets ruby act as a gain medium?

choices.text: Cr^3+
Al^3+
choices.why: Al^3+ belongs to the host crystal. The Cr^3+ impurities, which replace about 0.05% of the Al^3+ by mass, give ruby its gain.
Oxide ions are part of the Al2O3 host. The active ion in ruby is Cr^3+.

choices.text: Ti^3+
choices.why: Ti^3+ in Al2O3 is a different laser (780 nm in Table 15.5.1). In ruby the active ion is Cr^3+.

explanation: Ruby is Al2O3 in which Cr^3+ ions replace roughly 0.05% (by mass) of the Al^3+ ions. The electronic structure of these Cr^3+ impurities lets ruby act as a gain medium, lasing at 694.3 nm.

prompt: Why do ruby lasers use synthetic ruby rather than natural gemstones?

choices.text: Natural rubies have too many crystal defects
Natural rubies contain no chromium at all
choices.why: Natural ruby also contains Cr^3+. Synthetic ruby is used because natural stones have too many crystal defects.

choices.text: Synthetic ruby is a liquid at room temperature
choices.why: Synthetic ruby is a solid rod. It's chosen because natural rubies have too many crystal defects.

choices.text: Only synthetic ruby conducts an electric current
choices.why: Ruby is pumped by light from a flash lamp, not by a current. Synthetic ruby is used because natural rubies have too many crystal defects.

explanation: The Cr^3+ impurities make ruby a gain medium, but synthetic ruby must be used because natural rubies have too many crystal defects.

prompt: Table 15.5.1 lists Nd^3+ in three hosts: glass (1059 nm), YAG (1064.1 nm) and YLF (1054.3 nm). What does changing the host do?

choices.text: It shifts the wavelength slightly
It moves the light into the ultraviolet
choices.why: All three lines lie near 1060 nm, in the infrared. The host only shifts the wavelength by a few nm.

choices.text: It changes the active ion to Cr^3+
choices.why: The active ion is Nd^3+ in every case. Only the host changes, and with it the wavelength shifts slightly.

choices.text: It leaves the wavelength exactly the same
choices.why: The three wavelengths differ (1054.3 to 1064.1 nm), so the host does shift the line, though only slightly.

explanation: The same active ion, Nd^3+, lases at 1059 nm in glass, 1064.1 nm in YAG and 1054.3 nm in YLF. The host shifts the wavelength by only a few nm.

prompt: The Nd^3+:glass laser in Table 15.5.1 makes pulses lasting 1 ps (1.0 × 10^−12 s). Light travels at 3.0 × 10^8 m/s. How long is the stretch of light in one pulse, in mm? (Give it as a decimal.)
explanation: Distance = c × t = 3.0 × 10^8 m/s × 1.0 × 10^−12 s = 3.0 × 10^−4 m = 0.3 mm. A 1 ps pulse is a sliver of light less than a millimetre long.

prompt: Which gas-phase gain medium in Table 15.5.2 gives a continuous output?

choices.text: Ar^+, at 488 and 515 nm
N2, at 337 nm
choices.why: The N2 laser is listed as pulsed, with 1 ns pulses. Ion lasers such as Ar^+ run continuously.

choices.text: Cu, at 510 nm
choices.why: The copper laser is listed as pulsed, with 30 ns pulses. Ar^+ is listed as continuous.

choices.text: CO2, He and N2, near 10,000 nm
choices.why: The CO2 laser is listed as pulsed, with pulses longer than 100 ns. Ar^+ is listed as continuous.

explanation: In Table 15.5.2 the He–Ne, He–Cd, Ar^+ and Kr^+ lasers give continuous output, while the N2, Cu and CO2 lasers are pulsed.

prompt: The CO2 laser in Table 15.5.2 emits near 10,000 nm (1.0 × 10^−5 m). Using ν = c/λ with c = 3.0 × 10^8 m/s, what is the frequency of this light, in Hz? (Type it in scientific notation, like 2.5e13.)
explanation: ν = c/λ = (3.0 × 10^8 m/s)/(1.0 × 10^−5 m) = 3.0 × 10^13 Hz, an infrared frequency.

prompt: What is an exciplex?

choices.text: A gaseous species that exists only when excited
A dye molecule dissolved in a liquid organic solvent
choices.why: That's the gain medium of a dye laser. An exciplex, such as KrF*, is a gaseous species that forms and exists only in an excited state.

choices.text: A stable molecule that absorbs the pump light
choices.why: An exciplex isn't stable in the ground state; it forms and exists only in an excited state and falls apart when it emits.

choices.text: A crystal doped with a few metal ions
choices.why: That describes solid gain media such as ruby. An exciplex is a gaseous species, like XeCl*, that exists only in an excited state.

explanation: An exciplex is a gaseous species that forms and exists only in an excited state. Two common exciplex lasers are XeCl* (308 nm) and KrF* (248 nm).

prompt: Why is a population inversion automatic in an exciplex laser?

choices.text: The lower, dissociated state holds no molecules
The upper state decays faster than the lower one
choices.why: The key is that the lower state is dissociated: its partners fly apart, so it has no population at all, and any excited exciplexes are an inversion.

choices.text: The pump empties the ground state with a flash
choices.why: That is how ruby reaches its inversion. In an exciplex the lower state is dissociated, so it holds no population to begin with.

choices.text: The mirrors reflect away ground-state molecules
choices.why: Mirrors act on light, not on molecules. The inversion is automatic because the lower, dissociated state has no population.

explanation: Because only the upper, excited state can exist, there is no population in the lower, dissociated state, so a population inversion is obtained. The exciplex emits its excitation energy and falls apart at the same time.

prompt: KrF* lasers are often called excimer lasers. Why does the section say exciplex is the better name?

choices.text: KrF* is AB*, not an excited dimer AA*
KrF* exists only in its ground state
choices.why: KrF* exists only in an excited state. The naming point is that excimer means an excited dimer, AA*, while KrF* is made of two different atoms, AB*.

choices.text: Excimer lasers must use a liquid medium
choices.why: Excimer and exciplex lasers are both gas lasers. The issue is that an excimer is an excited dimer, AA*, but KrF* is AB*.

choices.text: Excimer refers only to dye molecules
choices.why: Excimer means excited dimer, AA*. KrF*, made of Kr and F, is AB*, which is an exciplex.

explanation: The term excimer refers to an excited dimer, AA*, so it should not be used to describe an exciplex, AB*, such as KrF* or XeCl*.

prompt: Two common exciplex lasers are XeCl* at 308 nm and KrF* at 248 nm. Since E = hc/λ, how many times greater is the energy of a KrF* photon than that of a XeCl* photon? (Give it as a decimal.)
explanation: E is proportional to 1/λ, so E(KrF*)/E(XeCl*) = 308/248 = 1.24. The shorter-wavelength KrF* photon carries about 24% more energy.

prompt: Why can a dye laser be tuned over a wide range of wavelengths?

choices.text: The dye has a broad emission band
The pump supplies many different excitation energies
choices.why: A single-wavelength pump is enough. Tunability comes from the dye's broad emission band, which provides gain over a wide range of wavelengths.

choices.text: The dye has just two sharp energy levels
choices.why: Two sharp levels would give one fixed wavelength. The dye's emission band is broad, which is what allows tuning.

choices.text: The mirrors change color as they warm up
choices.why: The mirrors don't set the color this way. The dye's broad emission band provides gain over a wide range, and a tuning element picks one wavelength.

explanation: The laser is tunable because the dye's broad emission band provides gain over a wide range of wavelengths. Rhodamine 6G, for example, can be tuned from 560 nm to 635 nm.

prompt: The laser dye rhodamine 6G can be tuned from 560 nm to 635 nm. How wide is this tuning range, in nm?
explanation: 635 nm − 560 nm = 75 nm of continuous tuning with a single dye.

prompt: In a tunable dye laser, how does the user choose the lasing wavelength?

choices.text: With a tuning element, often a movable grating
By changing the pump to the desired wavelength
choices.why: The pump wavelength doesn't set the laser wavelength. A tuning element in the cavity, often a movable diffraction grating, selects it from the dye's broad band.

choices.text: By heating the dye until its color changes
choices.why: Temperature isn't how the wavelength is chosen. A tuning element, often a movable diffraction grating, picks the wavelength.

choices.text: By taking out the output coupler mirror
choices.why: Without the output coupler no beam would leave the cavity. The wavelength is picked by a tuning element such as a movable diffraction grating.

explanation: The user chooses the desired lasing energy by means of a tuning element in the cavity, which is often a movable diffraction grating.

prompt: What is a solid state dye laser (SSDL)?

choices.text: A dye laser with the dye dispersed in a solid polymer
A dye laser whose dye solution has been frozen solid
choices.why: The dye isn't frozen. In an SSDL the dye is dispersed uniformly within a solid polymer matrix.

choices.text: A diode laser that uses an organic dye as its crystal
choices.why: Diode lasers use semiconductors such as GaAs. In an SSDL the dye is spread uniformly through a solid polymer matrix.

choices.text: A ruby laser with a dye coated onto its mirrors
choices.why: No ruby crystal is involved. In an SSDL the dye itself is the gain medium, dispersed in a solid polymer matrix.

explanation: In solid state dye lasers (SSDL), the dye is dispersed uniformly within a solid polymer matrix instead of being dissolved in a liquid.

prompt: Which of these does the section name as a way to pump a gain medium?

choices.text: Another laser, such as a diode laser
The output coupler
choices.why: The output coupler is a cavity mirror that lets light out. Pump energy comes from an electric current or an intense light source such as a flash lamp or another laser.

choices.text: A movable diffraction grating
choices.why: A grating is a tuning element that selects the wavelength. Pumps include electric currents, flash lamps and other lasers.

choices.text: Cooling the medium to a low temperature
choices.why: Cooling adds no energy. The pump must supply energy, for example an electric current, a flash lamp or another laser.

explanation: The energy for excitation is often supplied by an electric current or an intense light source, such as a flash lamp or an excitation laser. Diode lasers, excimer lasers and YAG lasers have all been used as pump sources.

prompt: Any laser could in theory be pulsed by delivering the pump energy in repeated bursts. Why can't every laser run as a continuous-wave (CW) laser?

choices.text: Some gain media can't keep a continuous inversion
CW lasers need a pump that flashes on and off regularly
choices.why: Repeated bursts give pulsed output. A CW laser needs the population inversion to be kept up continuously, which some gain media can't do.

choices.text: A continuous beam would melt the cavity mirrors
choices.why: Many lasers run continuously, such as the Ar^+ and Nd:YAG lasers. The limit is that some gain media can't sustain a continuous population inversion.

choices.text: Only liquid gain media can run continuously
choices.why: Solids (Nd:YAG) and gases (Ar^+) also run continuously. What matters is whether the medium can keep a population inversion continuously.

explanation: Not all lasers can operate as CW lasers, because in some gain media it is not possible to maintain a continuous population inversion. The ruby laser, for example, is very hard to run continuously and is almost always pulsed.

prompt: What forms a laser's optical (resonator) cavity?

choices.text: A pair of mirrors around the gain medium
A pair of lenses that focus the pump light
choices.why: Lenses don't form the cavity. A pair of mirrors on either side of the gain medium sends light back through it again and again.

choices.text: A sealed box that blocks all outside light
choices.why: The cavity isn't a light-tight box. It is a pair of mirrors that surround the gain medium and feed light back into it.

choices.text: The flash lamp and its reflector
choices.why: The flash lamp is a pump source. The cavity is the pair of mirrors that feed light back through the gain medium.

explanation: The optical cavity is formed by a pair of mirrors that surround the gain medium and feed light back into it. This feedback is critical, because it is where the amplification of the signal occurs.

prompt: Why is it critical that the cavity mirrors feed light back into the gain medium?

choices.text: Feedback is where the light gets amplified
The returning light cools the gain medium
choices.why: The light isn't there to cool anything. Each pass through the excited gain medium adds stimulated emission, so the feedback is where the amplification occurs.

choices.text: The returning light pumps the gain medium
choices.why: Pumping is the job of the separate pump source. The feedback sends light back through the medium so that it is amplified by stimulated emission.

choices.text: It keeps any light from leaving the laser
choices.why: Some light must leave, through the output coupler, to form the beam. The feedback matters because it is where the light is amplified.

explanation: The mirrors send the light back and forth through the gain medium, and on each pass stimulated emission adds to it. This feedback is where the amplification of the signal occurs, while the output coupler lets a portion out as the beam.

prompt: What is the output coupler of a laser cavity?

choices.text: A partly reflecting mirror that lets some light out
A fully reflecting mirror that keeps all the light in
choices.why: If all the light stayed in, there would be no beam. The output coupler reflects most light back but lets a portion leave the cavity.

choices.text: A lens that couples the pump light into the medium
choices.why: Pump light reaches the medium separately. The output coupler is the partly reflective mirror through which the beam leaves.

choices.text: A cable that couples the laser to its power supply
choices.why: The output coupler is an optical part, not an electrical one: a partially reflective mirror that lets part of the light out.

explanation: The output coupler is a partially reflective mirror. It lets a portion of the laser radiation leave the cavity but reflects most of the light back through the gain medium.

prompt: An output coupler reflects 98% of the light that strikes it back into the cavity and lets the rest out. If 50 W of light inside the cavity strikes it, how many watts leave as the laser beam?
explanation: The coupler transmits 100% − 98% = 2%, so 0.02 × 50 W = 1 W leaves. The other 49 W is reflected back through the gain medium.

prompt: What are the modes of a laser cavity?

choices.text: Standing waves of light trapped between the mirrors
The different ways the pump can be switched on
choices.why: Modes describe the light, not the pump. They are standing wave structures formed by light trapped between the mirrors.

choices.text: The quantized energy levels of the atoms in the gain medium
choices.why: Those are the atomic or molecular states. Modes are standing wave patterns of the light trapped in the cavity.

choices.text: Pulses that leave through the output coupler
choices.why: Modes are inside the cavity: standing wave structures of the light trapped between the mirrors.

explanation: The light trapped between the mirrors forms standing wave structures called modes.

prompt: In a diode laser, what serves as the optical cavity in place of separate mirrors?

choices.text: The polished end faces of the crystal
Nothing, since a diode laser has no cavity
choices.why: Without a cavity and stimulated emission a diode would just be an LED. The polished end faces of the semiconductor crystal form the cavity.

choices.text: A pair of external glass mirrors
choices.why: Diode lasers don't need separate mirrors: the polished end faces of the crystal reflect the light.

choices.text: The metal wires that carry the current
choices.why: The wires bring in the forward-bias current. The cavity is formed by the crystal's polished end faces.

explanation: Instead of separate mirrors, the polished end faces of the crystal form the optical cavity. The semiconductor's very high refractive index makes the abrupt change at these surfaces trap the photons in the crystal.

prompt: How is light produced in a GaAs diode laser?

choices.text: An electron and a hole recombine
A flash lamp excites Cr^3+ ions
choices.why: That is the ruby laser. In a semiconductor diode, light is emitted when an electron and a hole recombine and release energy as a photon.

choices.text: An exciplex emits and falls apart
choices.why: That is how exciplex lasers such as KrF* work. A diode emits when an electron and a hole recombine.

choices.text: A dye molecule emits in solution
choices.why: That is a dye laser. A diode emits light when an electron and a hole recombine in the semiconductor.

explanation: In diodes made of materials such as GaAs, the recombination of an electron and a hole releases energy in the form of a photon. Lasing in the diode is by stimulated emission.

prompt: How is a population inversion maintained in a diode laser?

choices.text: By a forward-bias current injecting electrons and holes
By a flash lamp firing repeatedly through the crystal
choices.why: Diode lasers are pumped electrically. A forward-bias current keeps injecting electrons and holes into the junction.

choices.text: By rapidly removing electrons that fall into holes
choices.why: Removing electrons would not invert anything. The inversion is kept up by a forward-bias current that keeps injecting electrons and holes.

choices.text: By cooling the crystal until it superconducts
choices.why: Superconductivity plays no role. A forward-bias current keeps supplying electrons and holes to the junction.

explanation: A population inversion is maintained by a forward-bias current that keeps injecting electrons and holes into the junction, where they recombine by stimulated emission.

prompt: GaAs diodes emit infrared light. How does the section say a diode can be made to emit red light instead?

choices.text: Dope it to make a material such as GaAs_(0.6)P_(0.4)
Run a much larger current through the GaAs crystal
choices.why: More current gives more light, not a new color. Changing the material, as in GaAs_(0.6)P_(0.4), changes the emission wavelength.

choices.text: Polish the crystal's end faces to a higher finish
choices.why: Polished faces form the cavity but don't set the color. A doped material such as GaAs_(0.6)P_(0.4) emits red light.

choices.text: Place a red color filter in front of the beam
choices.why: A filter can only block light, and GaAs emits no red light to pass. Doping, as in GaAs_(0.6)P_(0.4), shifts the emission to red.

explanation: GaAs emits infrared light, but it can be doped to create a material that emits at another wavelength. For example, GaAs_(0.6)P_(0.4) emits red light.

prompt: When an electron and a hole recombine in GaAs, the photon carries about 1.42 eV. Using λ (nm) = 1240/E (eV), what is the wavelength of this light, in nm?
explanation: λ = 1240/1.42 = 873 nm. That is past the red end of the visible, about 700 nm, which is why GaAs emits infrared light.
